analysis.one_liner: Bans refusing to rent or sell housing to people who pay with vouchers, benefits, or military service.
analysis.headline: Introduced on June 23, 2022, the bill was sent to the Senate Banking Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill adds three new protected classes to the Fair Housing Act, the federal law against housing discrimination. It would make it illegal to reject a renter or buyer because of where their money comes from — including Section 8 housing vouchers, Social Security or disability benefits, child or spousal support, or money from a relative or trust — and because they are a veteran or an active-duty service member. The bill never advanced past its first committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters and buyers whose income is legal but easy to screen out: families using federal, state, or local housing vouchers, people living on Social Security, disability (SSI), or Railroad Retirement benefits, recipients of child or spousal support, veterans, and active-duty service members. It also covers people whose rent is paid by a relative, guardian, or trust.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voucher holders, benefit recipients, veterans, service members

how_it_helps.text: Adds 'source of income' as a protected class under the Fair Housing Act, explicitly including Section 8 housing vouchers, federal, state, and local rental assistance, nonprofit rental subsidies, homeownership subsidies, Social Security and SSI benefits, Railroad Retirement benefits, child support, spousal support, and payments from a trust, guardian, conservator, cosigner, or relative.
Adds 'veteran status' and 'military status' as protected classes alongside race, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, and disability.

Extends the protections to the sale, rental, financing, and brokerage of housing, not just leases, and extends the federal law against intimidating people exercising their fair housing rights to the new classes.
Makes it illegal under existing fair housing enforcement mechanisms — which renters can invoke with HUD, state agencies, or the courts — rather than creating a new system.

analysis.who_pays: Rental property owners and others in the housing transaction chain who currently screen out tenants based on income source would have to accept voucher and benefit payments and treat them like wages. The cost is mostly administrative: adjusting screening practices and handling disputes. For some small landlords, accepting vouchers also means working with public housing agencies on inspections and payment timing.
analysis.who_pays_short: Rental property owners who screen out voucher tenants

drawbacks.text: The bill would require landlords, including small owners, to accept tenants whose income is a housing voucher or a government benefit, changing their screening practices and, in the case of vouchers, adding inspection and paperwork requirements that come with public housing agency administration.

It does nothing about the underlying funding limits of housing voucher programs — payment standards and waiting lists stay the same — so discrimination could still surface in subtler forms like credit standards or unit-by-unit pricing, and enforcement depends on underfunded fair housing agencies.
The bill also extends a federal certification window for state and local fair housing agencies to 40 months, a technical change whose effect is on agency administration rather than on renters.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection is meaningful and the cost is comparatively small. Voucher holders and people on fixed benefits regularly lose units they could afford because landlords refuse their payment source; making that refusal unlawful directly addresses it, using the existing Fair Housing Act enforcement structure. The burden falls on landlords' screening practices, which is real but administrative, and the bill's main weakness is that it does not address voucher funding or guarantee enforcement capacity.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which never held a hearing or vote on it, and it died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Tim Kaine introduced the Fair Housing Improvement Act of 2022 in the Senate on June 23, 2022, with seven original cosponsors.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
Eleven senators, all Democrats, cosponsored the bill.
No further action of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — appears in the bill's action history for the rest of the Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Rental property owners who refuse tenants paying with housing vouchers or living on benefits keep that ability, since no senator ever had to vote on the bill. With no recorded opposition, the bill died simply by never being taken up.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 11 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored, but the bill never got far enough for anyone to oppose it on the record.

industries.note: The bill would bar landlords from rejecting applicants because their income is a housing voucher, a government benefit, child support, or help from family — the screening practices many use today. Landlords who already accept vouchers would face more even competition with those who do not.

industries.industry: Real estate brokers and sales agents
industries.note: The non-discrimination rules would extend to home sales, financing, and brokerage, adding compliance obligations for agents and lenders handling income sources like benefits and support payments.
State and local fair housing agencies would gain a longer certification window (40 months) and a new set of protected classes to enforce, enlarging their role.
